s0.why: [1] calls calcite a carbonate mineral and the most stable polymorph of calcium carbonate; [2] says it is very common, particularly in limestone.

s1.why: [3] says calcite defines hardness 3 on the Mohs scale; [32]-[33] say its birefringence makes objects seen through a clear piece appear doubled.

s2.why: [45] says carbon dioxide released produces effervescence when calcite is treated with acid.

f0.why: [3] says calcite defines hardness 3 on the Mohs scale.

f2.why: [34] says the birefringent effect was first described by Rasmus Bartholin in 1669.

f3.why: [7] traces the name to the Latin word for lime, calx.

f4.why: [19] says its habits represent combinations of over 1000 crystallographic forms.

q1.why: [32] names birefringence (double refraction) and [33] says objects viewed through clear calcite appear doubled.

q2.why: [45] says the effervescence in acid comes from released carbon dioxide; [1] gives calcite as calcium carbonate.

q3.why: [3] says the Mohs scale is based on scratch hardness comparison.

q4.why: [6] says aragonite changes to calcite in days or less above 300 C; [5] makes aragonite a polymorph and [1] calcite the most stable one.

q5.why: [18] says colour is white or none but shades including orange occur when the mineral is charged with impurities.

q6.why: [2] says calcite is common as a component of limestone and [4] speaks of limestone composed mostly of calcite.
